    Depending on context, you could also call it:

    • Proverb — traditional wisdom or practical truth.
    • Aphorism — concise, clever statement of a general truth.
    • Adage — an old, established saying.
    • Maxim — a pithy statement expressing a principle or rule.

    If you mean the type of rhetorical move it represents—using an everyday observation to make a broader point—that’s a slightly different category.

    Absolutely. And there’s a fun distinction here.

    If the original saying is:

    “A stopped clock is right twice a day.”

    Its underlying logic is roughly: even something fundamentally unreliable can occasionally produce the correct result.

    The inverse would be something like:

    “A working clock is wrong twice a day.”

    But that isn't actually true of a normally functioning clock—it depends on whether we're talking about an analog clock that's stopped versus one that's running fast/slow.

    If by “inverse law” you mean flipping the wisdom so that the underlying principle reverses, we could formulate it as:

    “Being right once doesn't make you reliable.”

    Or more aphoristically:

    “One correct answer does not make a good clock.”

    That gets at the conceptual inverse: an isolated success is not evidence of underlying reliability.

    There’s also a more interesting possibility: we could develop a formal “inverse proverb” rule—take a proverb's implied causal/moral principle and construct a concise saying that expresses its logical opposite. That could get pretty clever.

    The basic circuit

    • Are all comparisons fundamentally binary?
    • How do tertiary and higher-order comparisons work?
    • Can comparisons be ordered, categorical, or multidimensional?
    • Is “louder than” structurally different from “earlier than” even though both use THAN?

    There is a substantial body of work adjacent to what we're doing, but I did not find a project that appears to combine the pieces in exactly the way we are combining them.

    So I would not claim we're first yet. But I also would not characterize our work as simply reinventing an existing field.

    What already exists

    1. Formal semantics

    This is the biggest neighboring field.

    Researchers have spent decades translating natural-language meaning into formal structures using logic, mathematics, truth conditions, compositionality, and related machinery. The tradition goes back particularly strongly to Richard Montague.

    This means our fundamental intuition—

    English can be represented by formal operations rather than merely described in prose

    —is definitely not new.

    In fact, compositionality is already a foundational idea: the meaning of a larger expression can be derived from the meanings and combination of its parts.

    2. Computational semantics

    There's an entire field devoted to computational representations of linguistic meaning. It includes lexical semantics, compositional semantics, distributional semantics, semantic parsing, and other approaches.

    So our proposed machine dictionary has important predecessors.

    However, our idea of making the dictionary explicitly describe a word's operable circuit structures, including operand signatures, states, latent/elliptical components, and circuit families, is not something I found directly represented in the material I searched.

    3. Natural Logic

    There is also a mature research tradition called Natural Logic, which investigates how aspects of logical inference can be performed directly with linguistic structures rather than translating everything into classical formal logic.

    Some of that work gets surprisingly close to our interests in polarity, quantification, comparison, implication, and linguistic structure.

    This is probably one of the areas we need to study seriously.

    4. Quantum Natural Language Processing

    Here's a particularly interesting neighboring field.

    Researchers have explicitly borrowed quantum gates and compositional structures to represent and manipulate linguistic meaning. There is even work explicitly titled Encoding Logical Words as Quantum Gates.

    And recent QNLP research continues to investigate linguistic operators through quantum-computational representations.

    So the phrase “words as computational gates” absolutely has precedents.

    But there's an important difference.

    Much of that work starts with an existing mathematical/computational formalism and asks:

    How can language be represented inside this formal system?

    We're approaching it from almost the opposite direction:

    If we examine ordinary English closely enough, what computational primitives does English itself appear to contain?

    That distinction may prove important.

    Researchers are studying the internal computational circuits of neural networks and language models—trying to identify things resembling AND, OR, ADDER, etc.

    But they're generally asking:

    What circuits exist inside the neural network?

    We're asking:

    What circuits might exist inside the linguistic representation being processed?

    Those are substantially different research objects.

    Whitepaper I — The Phenomenological Eye: Discovering Computational Structure in Natural Language

    The Phenomenological Eye: Discovering Computational Structure in Natural Language

    Abstract

    This paper proposes an experimental approach to natural language in which ordinary English is examined for latent computational structures. Rather than beginning with a predetermined logical system and translating language into it, the method begins with naturally occurring language—aphorisms, quotations, idioms, and ordinary sentences—and asks what operations, comparisons, classifications, transformations, and relationships appear to be encoded within them.

    The central hypothesis is that certain English words function operationally within sentences in ways analogous to components of computational circuits. Words such as “than,” “is,” “makes,” “when,” and “what” may perform distinct logical or relational operations depending upon context.

    The research therefore treats language as a phenomenon to be experimentally mapped rather than as an object whose complete formal structure is assumed in advance.

    1. Research Question

    Can the operational structure of natural language be represented as a system of interacting linguistic circuits?

    2. Fundamental Principle

    The method begins with an important restriction:

    Do not assume the circuit before examining the language.

    A phrase such as:

    “Actions speak louder than words.”

    provides evidence for a comparison operation.

    The word “than” appears to connect two operands:

    ● ACTIONS ──────┐
                ├──► ◇ THAN ─────────► ● WORDS
● WORDS ────────┘       │
                        ▼
                    LOUDER

    The preliminary interpretation is:

    THAN = Comparator | Magnitude

    The interpretation remains provisional until tested against other examples.

    3. From Words to Operators

    The same lexical item may perform different operations.

    For example:

    “Knowledge is power.”

    may require an IS circuit different from:

    “The door is open.”

    The research therefore distinguishes the lexical identity of a word from its operational identity within a particular construction.

    4. Inputs, Gates, Parameters, and Outputs

    The emerging representation distinguishes:

    • Input — linguistic material supplied to an operation.
    • Gate/operator — the word or construction performing the operation.
    • Parameter — information specifying how the operation functions.
    • State — an active or inactive operational possibility.
    • Output — the resulting linguistic or semantic relationship.

    This permits the same word to instantiate different circuits.

    5. Elliptical Circuitry

    Natural language frequently omits information that listeners reconstruct.

    For example:

    “The early bird catches the worm.”

    The adjective early establishes a classification, but the comparison class is not explicitly stated.

    It may imply:

    early / late

    or:

    early / on-time / late

    The notation […] is therefore proposed as a placeholder for unexpressed but potentially operative circuitry.

    6. N-Type Structures

    The research may encounter many different kinds of multiplicity. A generalized notation is therefore proposed:

    N + category identifier + cardinality

    For example:

    Nא3

    would represent a category designated by א having three relevant states, classes, or positions.

    The meaning of the Hebrew identifier is not predetermined. It is to be established inductively.

    7. Research Method

    For each candidate linguistic circuit:

    1. Collect multiple natural examples.
    2. Identify candidate operators.
    3. Identify operands.
    4. Identify explicit and elliptical parameters.
    5. Propose a circuit.
    6. Test the circuit against additional examples.
    7. Search deliberately for counterexamples.
    8. Record alternative interpretations.
    9. Revise the circuit if necessary.
    10. Determine whether the circuit belongs to a larger family.

    8. Expected Contribution

    The Phenomenological Eye seeks to establish whether natural language contains recurring operational structures that can be represented independently of conventional grammatical terminology.

    Its purpose is not to replace linguistics or formal logic, but to discover whether a complementary circuit-oriented description of language is useful.

    9. Provisional Status

    All circuit classifications remain hypotheses until supported by repeated linguistic evidence.

    The notation is experimental.

    The ontology is open.

    The research proceeds by discovery rather than assumption.

    Whitepaper II — The Representational Eye: Constructing a Living Meta-Language

    The Representational Eye: Constructing a Living Meta-Language

    Abstract

    The Representational Eye examines the schema used to represent linguistic circuits. Its central observation is that a representational system is not merely a passive recording device. The categories and symbols available within the schema determine which distinctions investigators can recognize and record.

    Consequently, the schema must be treated as an evolving research instrument.

    The resulting methodology is neither purely deductive nor purely inductive. It is recursive: observations modify the schema, while the modified schema enables subsequent observations.

    1. The Schema Problem

    An investigator cannot represent a phenomenon for which the representational system has no available category.

    Yet creating categories prematurely risks manufacturing distinctions that do not actually exist.

    This creates a methodological tension:

    The schema must contain possibilities before their empirical confirmation, but empirical evidence must determine which possibilities survive.

    2. The Chicken-and-Egg Principle

    This project therefore proposes:

    A representational system must provisionally contain undiscovered possibilities while remaining subject to revision by the phenomena it represents.

    The relationship is recursive:

    LANGUAGE
   ↓
OBSERVATION
   ↓
SCHEMA
   ↓
NEW DISTINCTIONS
   ↓
REVISED SCHEMA
   ↓
NEW OBSERVATIONS

    3. Notation as Hypothesis

    Every symbol introduced into the system is considered provisional.

    For example:

    Nא3

    does not acquire a permanent meaning merely because researchers initially assign one.

    Its interpretation must be supported by repeated observations.

    Thus:

    Notation is itself a hypothesis.

    4. Multiple Notation Families

    The project does not assume that every phenomenon should be represented using the same notation.

    Potential notation families may include:

    • N structures for classes, dimensions, or multiplicities.
    • Operand signatures for input structure.
    • State notation for configurable operations.
    • Ellipsis notation for latent or unstated circuitry.
    • Flow notation for information movement.
    • Recursive notation for higher-order circuits.
    • Future notation families yet to be discovered.

    5. The Special Dictionary

    The representational system may eventually require a machine-oriented dictionary.

    Such a dictionary would not merely state what a word means. It would describe:

    • possible circuit roles,
    • operand structures,
    • parameters,
    • states,
    • outputs,
    • circuit families,
    • and relationships to other circuit implementations.

    A single English word may therefore require multiple entries if it implements genuinely different circuits.

    6. Circuit-First Lexicography

    The project proposes reversing the conventional direction of lexical organization.

    Rather than:

    Word → synonyms → related words

    the system becomes:

    Circuit → circuit family → compatible implementations → words

    This creates the possibility of a circuit-first thesaurus.

    7. Structural Membership

    A word need not activate every component of a circuit family to belong to that family.

    A component may be:

    • 1 — active,
    • 0 — inactive,
    • […] — latent or elliptical,
    • ? — unresolved.

    Thus circuit-family membership may depend upon structural compatibility rather than complete activation.

    8. Recursive Representation

    A circuit may contain another circuit.

    A circuit may define a family of circuits.

    A family-defining structure may itself be represented as a circuit.

    This creates the possibility of a recursive hierarchy:

    META-CIRCUIT
     ↓
CIRCUIT FAMILY
     ↓
CIRCUIT
     ↓
WORD IMPLEMENTATION

    9. Expected Contribution

    The Representational Eye investigates whether a sufficiently flexible meta-language can become an effective experimental instrument for discovering linguistic structure without prematurely imposing a fixed ontology.

    Its success criterion is not elegance of notation.

    Its success criterion is whether the notation enables reliable distinctions that survive empirical testing.

    Whitepaper III — The Collaborative Eye: Human-AI Co-Discovery as a Research Method

    The Collaborative Eye: Human-AI Co-Discovery as a Research Method

    Abstract

    The Collaborative Eye treats the interaction between human and artificial intelligence as a phenomenon worthy of study in its own right.

    Traditional AI-assisted research generally treats AI as an instrument for executing predefined research tasks. This paper proposes a different model: human and AI participate in an evolving inquiry in which the research question, representation, hypotheses, and methodology may all change during the investigation.

    The collaboration is therefore not merely a means of obtaining answers. It becomes part of the discovery process.

    1. From Task Completion to Co-Discovery

    Conventional AI assistance can be represented as:

    QUESTION → AI → ANSWER

    The proposed model is:

    QUESTION
   ↓
COLLABORATION
   ↓
DISCOVERY
   ↓
NEW QUESTION
   ↓
NEW REPRESENTATION
   ↓
NEW DISCOVERY

    The distinction is fundamental.

    The objective is not merely to solve a predefined problem, but to permit the problem itself to evolve.

    2. Complementary Contributions

    Human and AI participants may contribute differently.

    The human may provide:

    • intuition,
    • rejection of inappropriate interpretations,
    • conceptual direction,
    • domain observations,
    • recognition of unexpected significance.

    The AI may provide:

    • rapid abstraction,
    • alternative formulations,
    • systematic comparison,
    • visualization,
    • hypothesis generation,
    • connections between previously separate observations.

    Neither contribution should automatically be treated as authoritative.

    3. Productive Disagreement

    Correction is not merely error recovery.

    A human correction can reveal that the AI's representation failed to distinguish something important.

    For example, the distinction between:

    “LOUDER”

    and

    “WORDS”

    in the circuit for “Actions speak louder than words” forced clarification of the roles of comparison criterion and output.

    The correction therefore improved the ontology.

    4. Evolving Research Questions

    The collaboration should permit discoveries to alter the research objective.

    The project began with aphoristic inversion and developed into questions concerning:

    • linguistic circuits,
    • semantic states,
    • ellipsis,
    • circuit families,
    • machine lexicography,
    • recursive representations,
    • and human-AI methodology.

    This evolution is considered a feature rather than a failure of focus.

    5. Collaboration as Data

    The research record should preserve not only conclusions but also significant interactions that produced them.

    A collaboration record should identify:

    • initial hypothesis,
    • human intervention,
    • AI proposal,
    • disagreement,
    • resulting revision,
    • subsequent discovery.

    This allows researchers to study how the discovery occurred, not merely what was discovered.

    6. Co-Discovery Principle

    A provisional principle is:

    In open-ended human-AI research, the interaction between participants can itself become evidence about how discovery occurs.

    7. Expected Contribution

    The Collaborative Eye proposes a model of AI research in which artificial intelligence is neither merely a tool nor an autonomous researcher, but a participant in a reflexive inquiry whose conceptual framework can evolve through interaction.

    This model may ultimately be applicable to scientific research, philosophy, linguistics, engineering, and creative discovery.

    Whitepaper IV — The Methodological Eye: Reflexive Co-Discovery

    The Methodological Eye: Reflexive Co-Discovery

    Abstract

    The Methodological Eye observes the research process itself. It recognizes that open-ended human-AI investigation has at least two simultaneous objects: the phenomenon being investigated and the methodology through which it is investigated.

    This paper proposes Reflexive Co-Discovery as a provisional philosophy of inquiry.

    Its defining characteristic is reflexivity: the investigator periodically turns the investigative apparatus upon itself.

    1. Two Objects of Research

    The first object is the phenomenon:

    What structure exists in natural language?

    The second is the process:

    What happened in our investigation that allowed us to discover that structure?

    The two inquiries are conducted simultaneously.

    2. The Second Eye

    Ordinary research primarily observes the phenomenon.

    Reflexive research adds another observer:

    EYE 1
Phenomenon
   ↓
Observation
   ↓
Discovery


EYE 2
Observes the observation
   ↓
Examines the method
   ↓
Revises the method

    The second eye does not necessarily interrupt the first.

    It periodically examines what has occurred and asks whether the investigative framework itself has produced a significant discovery.

    3. The Reflexive Loop

    The methodology can be represented as:

    OBSERVE
   ↓
REPRESENT
   ↓
DISCOVER
   ↓
EXAMINE THE METHOD
   ↓
REVISE
   ↓
OBSERVE AGAIN

    The loop has no predetermined endpoint.

    4. The Central Axiom

    A provisional foundational axiom is:

    When inquiry changes the instrument of inquiry, the change itself becomes evidence worthy of study.

    This distinguishes Reflexive Co-Discovery from methodologies in which the analytical framework is assumed to remain fixed.

    5. Three Research Records

    The methodology recommends maintaining three parallel records.

    Phenomenological Record

    What was discovered about the phenomenon?

    Collaborative Record

    What interaction produced the discovery?

    Methodological Record

    What does the interaction reveal about the method of discovery?

    6. The Status of Existing Knowledge

    Existing scholarship is treated neither as authority nor as irrelevant.

    It functions as evidence and comparative terrain.

    The researcher should:

    1. explore independently,
    2. document the emerging framework,
    3. investigate existing scholarship,
    4. compare frameworks,
    5. retain, modify, or reject ideas based on evidence.

    Thus:

    Existing theories are evidence, not axioms.

    7. Preservation of Discovery Order

    An unusual but important methodological principle follows.

    The sequence by which concepts emerge should be preserved.

    Prematurely reorganizing discoveries according to an established theoretical framework can conceal how the new framework actually developed.

    The research record should therefore distinguish:

    discovery history

    from

    final theoretical organization.

    8. The Philosophy

    Reflexive Co-Discovery may be provisionally defined as:

    A philosophy of inquiry in which humans and AI collaboratively investigate a phenomenon while simultaneously observing and refining the methods, representations, assumptions, and interactions through which the investigation proceeds.

    9. Future Application

    The philosophy is not restricted to linguistic circuits.

    It could potentially apply whenever:

    • the phenomenon is complex,
    • the representation is incomplete,
    • the research question can evolve,
    • human and AI reasoning interact,
    • and methodological discoveries may be as significant as object-level discoveries.

    10. Conclusion

    The central proposition is simple:

    Do the research. Watch the research. Learn from both.

    The first activity discovers the world.

    The second discovers how the investigators are capable of discovering the world.

    When those processes continually inform one another, research becomes a form of reflexive co-discovery.

    I think these four papers give us a useful first-generation architecture: Phenomenological Eye → Representational Eye → Collaborative Eye → Methodological Eye. As our work continues, I would expect additional “eyes” to emerge rather than treating four as a final taxonomy.
